articles.title: 1977: J&K’s Electoral Watershed

articles.html:
Jammu & Kashmir tasted its first ever legitimately free, fair election in 1977; a long 30 years after the rest of the country had gone through four periodic general elections, in 1957, 1962, 1967 and 1971.
The corresponding history of successive elections to 75-member J&K legislative Assembly during that period is riddled with instances of mass rigging, negligible voter participation (in Kashmir Valley) and brazenly manipulated election results.

Our very first election, for the state constituent assembly in 1951, held under Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s watch, was thoroughly rigged.
His successors, Bakhshi Ghulam Mohammad, Ghulam Mohammad Sadiq and Syed Mir Qasim followed suite ‘faithfully’; improvising upon the rigging techniques, election after election.The net result was that the ruling party won 100 percent seats in 1951 polls, 90 pc in 1957, 94 pc in 1962, 81 pc in 1967 and 60 pc in 1972. Number of uncontested seats was all 75 in 1951, 43 in 1957, 34 in 1962, 53 in 1967 and 5 seats in 1972.

Two notable political events of that period: (1) ruling NC under GM Sadiq merged itself in the Congress in 1964 while Bakhshi Ghulam Mohammad (then in opposition) retained the NC label and won 8 Assembly seats in the 1967 elections; and (2) in the very next election under Mir Qasim’s watch Jamat e Islami jumped into poll fray for the first time in 1972 winning 5 seats from the Valley. Syed Ali Shah Geelani being one of them.
Political grapevine has it that the JI freshers were ‘facilitated’ to win the seats held previously by the GM Sadiq’s supporters.

On the other hand, Sheikh’s Plebiscite Front was prevented from entering the election arena and outlawed soon after it declared its intention to contest 1972 assembly poll under oath of loyalty to the constitution.

Yet another ugly feature occurred in 1987 elections in which Farooq-led NC and Rajiv Gandhi-led Congress alliance was pitched against motley Kashmir-based secessionist combine, Muslim United Front (MUF). This time the rigging was shifted from polling booths to counting centers. Election results were manipulated in 10 to 15 constituencies in the Valley. In about a dozen constituencies the final number of rejected votes was more than the victory margin of ruling alliance candidates.
Mercifully, we have come a long way.Parliamentary polls and Assembly elections held in 2024 witnessed unprecedented high voter participation. However, pre-poll gerrymandering of constituencies is a fact though it didn’t yield any of its intended partisan gains. Even so, the conduct of elections was unquestionably free and fair.(It is in this jarring backdrop that the State’s first ever legitimate assembly election held in 1977 assumes extraordinary historical significance and deserves to be recalled, if only to remind ourselves as to how we reached where we stand today)July 9, 1977: A Landmark

Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah was today sworn-in as the Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir state, following his sweeping victory in the 1977 assembly elections, that had many firsts to its credit.
Sheikh’s swearing-in marked the end of the first-ever governor’s rule imposed in Jammu and Kashmir on March 26, 1977, following the withdrawal of Congress support to Sheikh Abdullah-led coalition government that itself was the political by-product of the Kashmir Accord of 1975.Governor LK Jha took over the reigns of the state administration with one Advisor, KT Satarawalla. Sushital Banerji was the chief secretary. Coincidentally, I was the Director of Information and Public Relations, on contract tenure, from which I resigned soon after the election process was over.Out of the total 76 assembly seats contested in the 1977 assembly election, the National Conference won 47, including 39 out of 42 seats in the Kashmir Valley, 7 out of 32 seats in Jammu and one out of the two seats in the Ladakh region.From the Valley, Abdul Ghani Lone from Langate and Abdul Rashid Kabli from Idgah managed to save their seats on the Janata Dal ticket while Syed Ali Geelani fielded by Jamat-e-Islami retained his Sopore seat.

Going back to history, the first elections held to the state constituent assembly in 1951, with Sheikh Abdullah as the state’s Prime Minister, were brazenly rigged with the ruling National Conference cornering all the 75 seats.

Sheikh’s post-1953 successor, Bakhshi Ghulam Mohammad won the assembly elections in 1957 and 1962 with newer techniques of rigging. Yet he was unceremoniously ejected from power in 1963 via Kamaraj Plan. His (unlikely) successor, Shamsuddin’s tenure was too short-lived as he had to make way for GM Sadiq within just a few months of a tentative rule, in the face of the Holy Relic agitation.
The 1967-elections held under Sadiq’s command saw record-breaking ‘theft’ of opposition candidates’ oath forms leading to their summary disqualification at the threshold.1972 elections held when Syed Mir Qasim had succeeded Sadiq were preceded by outlawing the Plebiscite Front even after it had declared its intention to swear allegiance to the Indian Constitution and to contest assembly polls.The sole credit for giving the people of this state their first genuinely free, fair election, in 1977, goes to the then prime minister Morarji Desai who put his foot down against the move by his Janata Party ministerial colleagues, Charan Singh and Jagjivan Ram to rig the polls and keep the Sheikh’s National Conference out of power.Polling was preceded by dirty campaigning with senior leading campaigners, mainly those from the New Delhi-blessed Janata Party headed in the state by Maulana Mohammad Sayeed Masoodi, berating a bed-ridden Abdullah.Campaigning for the NC fell on the shoulders of Mirza Afzal Beg who sought to counter the Janata Party assault with the display of ‘green handkerchief and rock salt’.

Beg, however, didn’t last long in the ruling set-up as the succession battle in the NC impelled his unceremonious exit from the party and its government within less than two years.
In 1977, the poll atmosphere was so surcharged that if Governor Jha, Advisor Satarawalla and chief secretary Sushital Bannerji had not acted tough to preserve administrative neutrality the NC with all its visible popular ground support could have found itself in the dumps.Credit primarily goes to the Chief Election Commissioner, Shyam Lal Shakder, a Kashmiri speaking renowned civil servant and former Lok Sabha secretary-general.In political terms, the difference in the political landscape in 1953 when Sheikh was dethroned and 1977 when he was back in the saddle, was that between chalk and cheese.

Given his tall political stature, the Sheikh, in his second term, had to awkwardly crawl and squeeze himself into the narrowed groove of his constitutional authority. (In a twist of fate, Sheikh’s 3G-successor, Omar today finds himself caged almost similarly with his administrative wings clipped. His resounding victory in 2024 notwithstanding.)

In today’s radically changed atmospherics it might sound incredible but it is true: in the 1977 elections, local political sensitivities still counted with those who were running the show here on behalf of ‘New Delhi’.

I vividly remember an instance. Governor LK Jha had prepared a draft television address to assure the people of Jammu and Kashmir that the election machinery would act fairly and that his interim administration would not take any major policy decision and would leave it to the coming legislature.
Jha was a renowned luminary. He had drafted an excellent (broadcast-cum-telecast) speech, yet he asked me to sit with him and feel free to suggest changes in the text; keeping local sensitivities in mind. I was overwhelmed by this gesture but was hesitant to go for any such ‘imprudent’ exercise.The Governor sensed my predicament and graciously asked me to carry the copy of the draft speech home and come back after suggesting changes. Somehow or the other, I mustered the strength to make certain substantial changes in the text, mainly to avoid the probable impression that the governor was trampling on the local sentiment and that the incoming elected government might feel short-changed. Jha not only approved the changes but thanked me for having done my duty as the governor administration’s PR chief.

After the installation of the Sheikh Abdullah-headed popular government, I put in my papers and returned to my profession.


Mohammad Sayeed Malik is a veteran journalist from Kashmir

articles.title: Safeguarding Childhood in the Digital Age
articles.description: In the heart of Srinagar, where the Jhelum River weaves through bustling markets and quiet neighborhoods, 13-year-old Ayesha sat cross-legged on her family’s worn rug, her eyes glued to her father’s o
articles.html:
In the heart of Srinagar, where the Jhelum River weaves through bustling markets and quiet neighborhoods, 13-year-old Ayesha sat cross-legged on her family’s worn rug, her eyes glued to her father’s old smartphone. The screen glowed with videos and messages from friends, a portal to a world beyond punctuated life in Jammu and Kashmir (J&K). Her mother, Rubina, watched from the kitchen, a flicker of worry crossing her face. Like many parents in J&K, Rubina knew the internet was a double-edged sword, a gateway to learning but also a minefield of dangers for her daughter. 

Ayesha’s story is not unique. Across J&K, children are diving headfirst into the digital age. Smartphones and cheap data plans have brought the internet to urban centers and remote villages alike, with internet penetration soaring in recent years. But with this connectivity comes a shadow. Cybercrimes in J&K jumped from 120 cases in 2020 to 173 in 2022, according to the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB). For children, the risks are even more insidious, cyberbullying, online predators, deepfakes, and misinformation lurk behind every click. 

Rubina’s unease grew after hearing whispers of a local teen tricked by an online scammer posing as a friend. She had learned at a community meeting that cybercrime against children nationwide had spiked over 400% between 2020 and 2024, often involving explicit material or grooming. An analysis of the latest NCRB data by CRY (Child Rights and You) shows 1,238 cases were registered under the Information Technology Act in connection with cybercrimes against children in 2024. Consistently, nearly 9 in every 10 reported incidents involve online child sexual exploitation as per NCRB data, with thousands of cases registered under the Information Technology (IT) Act. J&K’s numbers were murkier, but the trend was clear: children were vulnerable. The recent cybercrime trends revealed by NCRB once again underscore why children’s safety in the online space must remain a national priority. 
Rubina, a seamstress with no tech background, felt powerless. How could she protect Ayesha when she barely understood the internet herself? Roughly only 40% of Indians can handle basic digital tasks, and in J&K that number likely dips lower. 

Yet hope was stirring. In December 2023, in the University of Kashmir’s auditorium, experts at a CyberPeace Foundation with active participation of officials and functionaries and field staff of Mission Vatsalya (erstwhile ICPS), Department of Social Welfare, UT of J&K, had a dialogue and laid bare J&K’s digital challenges. They spoke of deepfakes twisting young minds and the urgent need for laws like the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, to shield privacy of the children. They called for local solutions, workshops, school programs, and tech tools tailored to J&K’s unique landscape. Rubina, though not at the event, heard about it through a neighbor. It sparked an idea: maybe she and Ayesha could learn together. The law, at least, was on their side. India’s Information Technology Act, 2000, cracks down on Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), while the POCSO Act, 2012, offers a child- friendly way to report online abuse. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, protects vulnerable kids, and the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, along with the 1098 and 1930 helplines, provides ways to fight back. However, a report from Kashmir Dispatch suggests that in J&K, enforcement lags, only 53 of 2022’s 173 cybercrime cases reached the chargesheet stage with only single conviction. Rubina wondered if these laws could truly reach her corner of Srinagar! 

One evening, Ayesha came home buzzing about a school workshop. A teacher, trained through a Digital India initiative, had shown her class how to spot phishing links and set privacy controls on apps. Ayesha proudly showed Rubina how to activate YouTube Kids, with its parental controls to  filter content. The workshop was part of a broader push: schools across J&K were starting to weave online safety into lessons, urged by the Ministry of Education. 
Rubina decided to act. She joined a community group where parents shared tips on monitoring screen time and recognizing cyberbullying. She learned about child-friendly apps and the importance of open conversations with Ayesha about her online world. Meanwhile, J&K’s government, spurred by events like the CyberPeace dialogue, was working with the National Informatics Centre to stabilize internet access and secure digital infrastructure. Plans were afoot for dedicated cybercrime units, inspired by the CBI’s Cyber Crime Investigation Cell, to tackle cases involving kids. 

Tech companies were stepping up too. Platforms were rolling out age-appropriate filters, nudged by global standards like the UK’s Age-Appropriate Design Code. In J&K, advocates pushed for tools in local languages to reflect the region’s diversity. For kids like Ayesha, especially orphans or those scared by other emergent exigencies, the Mission Vatsalya through its district wise Child Welfare Committees and Child Protection Units, promised extra support, through its rollout needed urgency. 

As winter settled over Srinagar, Rubina felt a shift. Ayesha still loved her smartphone, but now she navigated it with caution, armed with lessons from school and talks with her mom. Rubina, once daunted, felt empowered, part of a growing network of parents, educators, and policymakers weaving a safety net for J&K’s kids. Dr. Shazia Manzoor, a local educator, captured it best: “Prioritizing child safety in the digital landscape paves the way for a future where our youth can explore the vast potential of the online world securely.” 

Ayesha’s story is J&K’s story, a tale of vulnerability but also resilience. By blending digital literacy, stronger laws, better infrastructure, and community action, J&K can shield its children from the internet’s perils. The path isn’t easy, but with every workshop, every helpline call, every parent like Rubina who learns to guide their child, the region edges closer to a safer digital dawn. For Ayesha and thousands like her, that’s a future worth building.

Author is associated with the Juvenile Justice System.
(Note: Names are not real)

articles.title: Kashmir’s beauty deserves better
articles.description: As someone born in Srinagar, I have always taken immense pride in calling Kashmir my birthplace. Every visit to the Valley rekindles cherished memories and reinforces my emotional bond with its majest
articles.html:
As someone born in Srinagar, I have always taken immense pride in calling Kashmir my birthplace. Every visit to the Valley rekindles cherished memories and reinforces my emotional bond with its majestic mountains, crystal-clear rivers, verdant meadows, and serene lakes. Sadly, my recent visit left me with emotions very different from those I had anticipated.

During my travels through Srinagar, Pahalgam, Sonmarg, Baramulla and Aharbal, I was deeply distressed by the widespread presence of plastic waste. PET bottles, snack wrappers, plastic bags and other non-biodegradable refuse lay scattered along roads, tourist destinations and public spaces. Nothing, however, was more heartbreaking than seeing plastic waste strewn along the banks of the pristine River Sind, a river whose crystal clear water has long symbolised the purity and grandeur of Kashmir.

The sight was painful not merely because it offended the eye, but because it reflected a growing indifference towards one of nature’s greatest gifts. Plastic pollution is no longer merely an aesthetic concern. It threatens rivers, forests, wildlife, agriculture, tourism and, ultimately, human health. If allowed to continue unchecked, it will irreversibly diminish the very beauty that draws millions of visitors to Kashmir every year.

Being a Senior Advocate, the first thought that crossed my mind was to invoke the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh by filing a Public Interest Litigation. I immediately commenced the necessary groundwork. However, I soon learnt that a Public Interest Litigation concerning this very issue is already pending before the Hon’ble High Court. I have implicit faith that the matter is being pursued in the right earnest and that appropriate directions will be issued to strengthen environmental protection and waste management in the Union Territory.
Judicial intervention, however, can only provide part of the solution. Courts may issue directions, governments may frame policies, and municipal authorities may strengthen enforcement, but lasting change can only come when society itself embraces environmental responsibility.

That responsibility must begin with our children.
Environmental education should become an integral part of the school curriculum throughout Jammu & Kashmir. Students must be sensitised from an early age to the devastating consequences of environmental degradation, particularly the menace of plastic pollution. They should learn not only why plastic waste is harmful but also how it should be segregated, recycled and responsibly disposed of. Habits formed in childhood often endure for life, and today’s environmentally conscious students will become tomorrow’s responsible citizens.

Tourists, too, must recognise that visiting Kashmir is a privilege that carries corresponding responsibilities. Every discarded bottle or wrapper diminishes the natural heritage they have come to admire. Likewise, local communities, businesses, hoteliers, transport operators and tour organisers must work together to ensure that cleanliness becomes as much a part of the Kashmir experience as its unparalleled hospitality.

The administration undoubtedly bears the primary responsibility of providing adequate waste collection, segregation and recycling infrastructure. Visible enforcement against littering, coupled with sustained public awareness campaigns, will go a long way in changing public behaviour. Yet governmental action alone cannot preserve paradise. Every citizen has a role to play.

Kashmir has survived centuries of political upheaval, natural disasters and human conflict. Surely, we must not allow plastic waste to become another scar upon its incomparable landscape.

If we genuinely believe that Kashmir is “Paradise on Earth”, then preserving its rivers, lakes, forests and valleys is not merely an administrative obligation but a moral duty that we owe to future generations. The Valley has given us beauty beyond measure. It is time for all of us, government, judiciary, educational institutions, civil society, residents and tourists alike to give something back.

Let us ensure that the next generation inherits a Kashmir whose splendour is remembered not through photographs and poetry alone, but through the living reality of a clean, green and unspoiled paradise.

Kamal Nijhawan, senior advocate practising before Supreme Court of India & Delhi High Court, was born in Srinagar, Kashmir and had his schooling, college & university education in the valley.
